# Grupo Frontera Political Controversy

## Origins of the Controversy

The political controversy surrounding Grupo Frontera emerged in early 2025, stemming from a confluence of viral social media content and a climate of heightened political tension within the United States , . The Texas-based norteño band, composed of Adelaido 'Payo' Solís III, Juan Javier Cantú, Julián Peña, Alberto Acosta, Carlos Guerrero, and Brian Ortega, had established itself as a prominent cultural force with strong ties to both the U.S. and Mexico, particularly through their breakthrough hit "No Se Va" . Their public image was built on themes of cross-border identity and supporting Mexican immigrants, which made them a target for intense scrutiny when allegations of political disloyalty surfaced . The controversy was not ignited by a single event but rather by three interconnected catalysts that, when viewed together, created a powerful narrative of betrayal among their core audience. The first and most immediate trigger was a now-deleted TikTok video that circulated widely in early 2025 , . In the clip, the band members were seen dancing backstage to the Village People's 1978 disco anthem "Y.M.C.A." , . The critical element of this video was not the act of dancing itself, but the song's growing association with the presidency of Donald Trump . Since at least 2020, "Y.M.C.A." had become a staple at Trump rallies, transforming the innocuous pop song into a potent political symbol . The timing of the video's circulation, coinciding with the aftermath of the November 2024 U.S. presidential election, was crucial, as it occurred amidst widespread fear within Latino communities about potential large-scale deportations under a second Trump administration , .

The second, and arguably more damaging, catalyst was a separate viral video showing the grandmother of one of Grupo Frontera's members celebrating Donald Trump’s victory in the 2024 U.S. presidential election , , . This individual became known to the public as "La Abuela Frontera," creating an undeniable and personal link between the band's private life and the controversial political figure who had promised harsh immigration policies . Her public display of joy over Trump's win resonated deeply with fans, who interpreted it as an endorsement of his platform by the artist group she represented. This piece of evidence was particularly powerful because it seemed to confirm the suspicions fueled by the "Y.M.C.A." video, suggesting a unified sentiment within the band's inner circle that contradicted their public persona as defenders of immigrants. A third contributing factor that amplified speculation was a clip of the band members evading questions during an interview concerning the ongoing U.S.–Mexico border crisis . While not inherently incriminating, such evasiveness in a high-profile situation often fuels conspiracy theories and leads audiences to fill the silence with their own interpretations, especially when other negative signals are present . Together, these three elements—a popular dance trend associated with a political movement, a family member's explicit celebration of that movement's leader, and ambiguous public statements—created a perfect storm of misinterpretation. The controversy erupted immediately following the November 2024 election, quickly escalating into a full-blown public relations crisis that threatened the band's reputation and fan base .

This complex set of circumstances positioned Grupo Frontera at the center of a highly charged political debate. Their carefully cultivated identity as authentic representatives of the borderlands, whose music often championed immigrant struggles, made any perceived deviation from this stance a profound shock to their supporters. The combination of these viral moments, occurring in a period of acute political anxiety, ensured that the controversy would spread rapidly across social media platforms, setting the stage for a significant public backlash.

## Public Backlash and Fan Reaction

The public reaction to the emerging controversy was swift, severe, and overwhelmingly negative, framed by many fans as an act of profound betrayal . The backlash was not merely a disagreement over political opinions; it was a visceral rejection rooted in feelings of abandonment by a culturally significant artist group whose identity was intrinsically linked to the struggles of the Mexican and Latino community . Fans accused the group of being traitors, labeling them "Trump Supporters" and questioning their authenticity and loyalty . The sentiment was captured in strong language used in online discussions, including slogans like "We should cancel them all" and "Never come back to Mexico," which underscored the deep sense of grievance felt by a substantial portion of their fan base . This intense response was fueled by the perception that Grupo Frontera, by implication, supported a political party whose platform included large-scale deportations targeting Latinos , . The controversy led to widespread calls for the group's "cancellation," a term indicating a demand for their removal from cultural and commercial spaces .

The backlash manifested in concrete, organized actions that demonstrated its seriousness and reach. A significant example was a Change.org petition demanding that Grupo Frontera be removed from the lineup of the Sueños Music Festival in Chicago , . The petition, which gained considerable traction, explicitly cited the band's alleged support for Donald Trump as incompatible with Latino values . It claimed the group had been "caught and found out to be Trump Supporters" and threatened a broader boycott of the festival if the band remained on the schedule . The petition's success was notable; it collected over 10,400 signatures, indicating a massive groundswell of opposition . One petitioner, a man from Chicago who had paid over $800 for tickets, articulated a clear economic motive behind his participation, stating he sought a refund due to the band's perceived "shift in ideology" . The existence of this petition, confirmed by Billboard magazine, marked the transition of the controversy from mere social media outrage to organized activism with tangible consequences . The group itself acknowledged the petition's existence and its impact, confirming that the feedback from their audience was influencing their response strategy .

The intensity of the criticism directed at Grupo Frontera was reported to be exceptionally high, surpassing the level of backlash experienced by other prominent Latin artists who had also faced scrutiny, such as Anuel AA, Justin Quiles, Lili Estefan, and Myrka Dellanos . This suggests that the unique combination of the band's immense popularity, their self-proclaimed immigrant identity, and the specific nature of the evidence created a uniquely volatile situation. Their public persona as "los hijos del norte" (the children of the north/border) made accusations of betrayal particularly stinging, as it implied a fundamental dishonesty about their roots and experiences . The group remained largely silent in the initial phase of the controversy, with no public response issued until late February 2025, a period during which the fan anger continued to fester and grow . This silence likely exacerbated the situation, as it allowed rumors and negative narratives to proliferate without direct rebuttal. The collective fury of their core audience, combined with organized efforts like the festival petition, placed the band in a precarious position, forcing them to confront the severity of the crisis head-on.

## Grupo Frontera's Response and Clarifications

Grupo Frontera's response to the escalating controversy was deliberate, multi-pronged, and evolved over time to systematically address the various facets of the accusations leveled against them. Their strategy began with immediate damage control aimed at severing any perceived political affiliations, followed by direct refutations of specific misconceptions, and ultimately culminated in a series of proactive actions intended to rebuild trust with their audience. The first official statement was released on February 7, 2025, via an Instagram Story , . This initial communication was direct and unequivocal, designed to establish a clear boundary between the band and any political party deemed hostile to immigrants. The statement read, "We want to clarify that Grupo Frontera has NO affiliation nor alliance with any political party that’s against immigrants and the Latino community" , . This opening line was a strategic move to preemptively neutralize the core accusation of supporting a Trump-aligned agenda. The statement then directly addressed the most sensitive aspect of the controversy by separating the band's identity from that of their families, stating, "It’s important you know that the opinions of our friends and family don’t represent Grupo Frontera" , . This was a direct acknowledgment of the "La Abuela Frontera" incident, attempting to depersonalize the conflict and assert that the celebratory actions of a relative did not constitute the band's official position. Finally, the statement reaffirmed their foundational identity, declaring, "we are immigrants, we are from the border, and Grupo Frontera will always be by and for the people" , . This closing remark was a powerful rhetorical device, appealing to their core values and the very identity that had made them beloved by their audience.

As the controversy persisted, the band issued further clarifications, most notably addressing the "Y.M.C.A." dance that had become the centerpiece of the backlash. On February 22, 2025, they released an Instagram video that directly confronted the viral clip . In this video, lead singer Adelaido 'Payo' Solís and percussionist Julian Peña Jr. explained that the dance was not a political statement but rather a pre-show routine that the group had performed since their childhood days in primary school , . This explanation was crucial because it provided an alternative, apolitical origin story for the viral moment, effectively dismantling the central piece of evidence used by their critics. By framing it as a nostalgic, non-political habit, they sought to strip the act of its coded meaning and restore its original, innocent intent. Payo Solís also clarified in this statement that only the six official members of the group speak on behalf of Grupo Frontera, further distancing themselves from external voices and reinforcing the idea that the actions of family members were not representative of the band's collective stance . The tone of this response shifted slightly from the initial blunt denial to a more explanatory and even lamentful one, with Peña Jr. concluding, "We are migrants. We’re for migrants. We always have been," while also expressing sorrow that "fake news" had turned the community "against our own people" , .

Months later, in June 2025, the band took a significant step beyond mere denials and explanations by engaging in tangible action to demonstrate their commitment to their stated values. In a public Instagram post, they expressed solidarity with immigrant communities affected by ICE raids across the United States, including those in Los Angeles and Texas . The statement conveyed empathy, saying, "As immigrants, we understand the pain, uncertainty, and fear that many are experiencing" . Crucially, they followed this expression of solidarity with a concrete plan of action: they announced that they would donate a portion of all proceeds from their surprise EP, *Y Lo Que Viene*, to frontline organizations providing support to migrant communities impacted by immigration enforcement . This move transformed their response from purely defensive to proactive and supportive. It allowed them to align their actions with their words, offering a form of restitution and rebuilding credibility through philanthropy. This layered strategy—from immediate denial to myth-busting clarification and finally to demonstrable support—illustrated a sophisticated approach to managing a modern brand crisis in the digital age, aiming not just to quell the firestorm but to begin the long process of healing the relationship with their audience.

## Broader Context and Nuanced Positions

To fully comprehend the magnitude of the "Grupo Frontera political controversy," it is essential to analyze the broader context that shaped both the controversy and the band's identity. The group's public persona was fundamentally built upon their lived experience as immigrants from the U.S.-Mexico border, a theme that permeates their music and public statements , . This self-identification as "migrants" and "from the border" was not merely a marketing tool but a core part of their artistic mission, positioning them as authentic voices for the Mexican and Latino communities . Therefore, the accusations of betrayal were particularly potent because they challenged the very foundation of the band's legitimacy in the eyes of their supporters. The controversy unfolded against a backdrop of national anxiety, specifically related to the policies of the incoming Trump administration following the November 2024 election , . Campaign promises to initiate large-scale deportations created a palpable sense of fear and vulnerability within Latino communities across the United States, making any perceived alignment with such a platform a matter of grave concern , . The controversy, therefore, was less about abstract political theory and more about the real-world implications of those theories for a community that felt directly threatened.

In addition to the high-stakes political environment, an EL PAÍS interview conducted around the time of the controversy provides valuable insight into the band's nuanced and pragmatic positions on complex issues like immigration and the U.S.-Mexico border wall . During the interview, the members articulated a careful balance between respecting the laws of the country they live in and advocating for their immigrant community. They stated, "We respect American laws, but we support Mexican immigrants as best we can" . This phrasing reveals a desire to navigate the difficult realities of living on both sides of the border without taking an overtly confrontational or simplistic political stance. Their discussion of the physical barrier further illustrates this complexity. When asked about the border wall, band member Beto (Alberto Acosta) initially rejected the idea, saying, "No… but at the end of the day, there’s no wall" . However, another member, Julián Peña Jr., offered a more grounded perspective, noting, "there is [a wall], but only halfway. They never finished it. And that’s where we live," referring to the incomplete construction of the barrier in the Rio Grande Valley near their hometown . This exchange highlights their lived reality: the wall is a tangible, fragmented presence in their daily lives, not just a distant political abstraction. The band also cited past actions, such as visiting a community center in 2023 to donate toys for children of detained migrants, as evidence of their consistent support for immigrants . These statements and actions paint a picture of a group that actively engages with the challenges facing their community, albeit through a lens of practicality and cultural pride rather than overt political activism.

This broader context explains why the controversy struck such a nerve. For their fans, Grupo Frontera was not just a musical act; they were seen as cultural ambassadors representing a shared struggle and identity. The band's initial, staunchly pro-immigrant messaging had created an implicit contract with their audience. When the viral videos appeared, they were interpreted as a breach of that contract, a sign that the band's public message was a facade hiding a different, and potentially hostile, reality. The backlash was thus a defense mechanism for the community, an attempt to protect their symbolic representation from what they perceived as a dangerous ideological shift. The band's subsequent responses, particularly their emphasis on their immigrant identity, were attempts to re-anchor themselves in this same cultural territory, reassuring their audience that their core identity remained unchanged despite the accusations. Understanding this dynamic—of a band whose identity is inseparable from their community, and a community whose security is tied to the perceived loyalty of its cultural icons—is key to understanding the emotional weight and political gravity of the controversy.

## Aftermath and Legacy

The aftermath of the "Grupo Frontera political controversy" saw the band navigating a delicate path of reconciliation with a segment of their audience that had felt profoundly betrayed. While the provided sources do not offer a comprehensive analysis of the long-term career impacts, they detail the resolution of the most immediate and visible consequence of the backlash: the organized petition against their performance at the Sueños Music Festival in Chicago , . The band confirmed the existence of the petition and its influence on their communications strategy, acknowledging the depth of their fans' concerns . Ultimately, the petition succeeded in having the band removed from the festival's lineup, marking a tangible loss for the group. However, the band's sustained response, which evolved from initial denials to a demonstrable act of solidarity through their donation initiative, appears to have been effective in mitigating the most severe aspects of the public relations crisis . By publicly committing to support frontline organizations aiding immigrants, they transformed the narrative from one of denial to one of active advocacy, providing a new basis for their relationship with their supporters .

The legacy of this event serves as a significant case study in the dynamics of modern celebrity, social media, and political polarization. It highlights how in a hyper-connected world, seemingly innocuous actions or pieces of content can be decontextualized and weaponized, taking on meanings far removed from their original intent , . The controversy underscored the immense power of symbolic interpretation, where the act of dancing to a particular song became a proxy for a much larger and more contentious political allegiance . For Grupo Frontera, it demonstrated that an artist's public identity, particularly one built on authenticity and cultural representation, is fragile and can be challenged by the very symbols they use. The band's experience also illustrates the sophistication required in modern crisis management, showcasing a response that progressed from damage control to myth-busting and finally to restorative action through philanthropy.

For their audience, the controversy exposed the deep anxieties and political divisions within the Latino community in the United States, particularly regarding immigration policy and the threat of deportation , . The intense backlash revealed that for many fans, an artist's cultural identity and political stance are inextricably linked, and any perceived disloyalty is met with swift and organized resistance. The episode highlighted the role of fan communities as active agents in policing the political correctness of their cultural icons, capable of mobilizing significant pressure through online petitions and social media campaigns , . In conclusion, while the immediate fallout resulted in the band's removal from a major festival, their multi-faceted response likely helped to preserve their core fan base and reaffirm their commitment to their community. The controversy remains a defining moment in their career, illustrating the profound intersection of art, identity, and politics in contemporary society.

A rundown of Grupo Frontera’s most highly scrutinized online political comments and non-comments

Grupo Frontera gets that people want to ask them about the U.S.-Mexico border: look at their name and look at the current [political climate](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2025-03-05/trumps-address-to-congress-revived-false-or-misleading-claims-on-immigration). They mostly just don’t want to talk about that.

But behind the line of questioning have been the [rumors](https://www.tiktok.com/@alexgootz/video/7465856247015755013) [swirling](https://www.tiktok.com/@aldoandheather/video/7465286279681428782) [online](https://www.tiktok.com/@alondracosilionn/video/7468870894442532102) that the Grupo Frontera members and those related to its members voted for and supported President Trump in the 2024 presidential election. The speculation has forced the “Tulum” performers to deny any affiliations with any political parties several times over.

So ahead of the Norteño band’s upcoming gig at SXSW on March 14, here’s a refresher of turbulent 2025 online discourse the Texas artists have found themselves at the center of.

In an interview with [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/grupo-frontera-sxsw-billboard-cover-1235914782/) published Tuesday, the group was asked whether or not its felt the effects of the political moment.

“I mean, our group name, Grupo Frontera, I think it feels natural for people to be like, ‘You’re from the border,’ stuff like that,” drummer Carlos Guerrero said in section of the interview that was notably conducted in December. “We always try to keep that private.” Percussionist Julian Peña Jr. added the group aims to “talk about music, that’s it.”

But this was far from the first time the “No Se Va” singers have been asked about or been placed in a situation where they’ve been forced to talk about the U.S. political situation. It does, however, follow a pattern of nondescript answers that the group’s members have previously been provided.

### [The Música Mexicana revolution shaping Southern California](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2024-09-19/the-musica-mexicana-revolution-shaping-socal)

Música Mexicana has been pushed into the mainstream over the last five years by Gen Z and millennial Latino audiences. Here’s a guide on the genre’s essential instruments, where to find the best música Mexicana-themed parties, where to shop for the perfect vaquero outfit and more.

Sept. 19, 2024

In a now-deleted TikTok video that circulated earlier this year, Grupo Frontera was shown dancing to the Village People’s mega hit “Y.M.C.A.” This concerned fans of the band online because of the song’s heavy association with [Donald Trump rallies](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-10-16/trump-cognitive-ability-rally-music), which the politician has used at his events since [at least 2020](https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/tv/story/2020-10-19/trump-dancing-rally-seinfeld-julia-louis-dreyfus).

Around the time that the “Y.M.C.A.” video circulated, Grupo Frontera was announced as the headliners at the Sueños music festival in Chicago. Soon after the announcement, a [Change.org petition](https://www.change.org/p/remove-grupo-frontera-from-sue%C3%B1os-lineup) was started that called for the band to be removed from the festival lineup and has collected over 10,400 signatures.

The Chicago man who started the online campaign said he paid over $800 and wanted a refund due to what he believed was the band’s shift in ideology, according to the [Chicago-Sun Times](https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/suenos-music-festival-chicago/2025/02/11/grupo-frontera-trump-suenos-petition-festival-chicago-ymca). The man admitted that the video of the group dancing to “Y.M.C.A” did not mention Trump or express any overt political views, but he noted that the timing of the post felt significant to him.

Oct. 19, 2020

Following the circulation of the video, the group’s social media posts became filled with comments such as: “You guys should start singing in English,” “In Mexico we don’t forgive,” and “Let’s stop supporting a group that is anti-Mexican.”

The hitmakers seemingly responded to the online backlash they were receiving in a social media post.

“We want to clarify that Grupo Frontera has NO affiliation not alliance with any political party that’s against immigrants and the Latino community,” the group wrote in a Feb. 7 Instagram story. “Like many of you, our families and \[group\] members have fought and struggled for a better future, and we will always take our people’s side, defending our roots and values.”

The band continued, “It’s important you know that the opinions of our friends and family don’t represent Grupo Frontera. We are immigrants, we are from the border, and Grupo Frontera will always be by and for the people.”

(Trump was not mentioned in the band’s statement.)

In the year since Grupo Frontera’s inception, the McAllen, Texas, players have made enormous strides — not just for themselves but for the regional Mexican genre.

May 4, 2023

“We dedicate ourselves to music. We love everyone and want peace and love. Take care of yourselves,” Peña Jr. responded.

Social media personality and immigrant rights activist [Carlos Eduardo Espina](https://www.tiktok.com/@carlos_eduardo_espina), who touts 12.3 million TikTok followers, was among the [many](https://www.tiktok.com/@antonioamex1/video/7465406578057940255) [people](https://www.tiktok.com/@therealkatherine/video/7465576786303208747) [upset](https://x.com/suaonthemoon/status/1884661389781786645) online and responded to the clip of the red carpet moment with a loud condemnation of Peña Jr.’s comments.

“For me, this was one of the worst responses that I have ever seen to a question in my whole life,” Espina said in a [Feb. 21 TikTok video](https://www.tiktok.com/@carlos_eduardo_espina/video/7473892359663652126). “Just like the saying goes, there are times when not saying anything says a lot. ... what an embarrassment.”

Following that round of online criticism Grupo Frontera decided to address the situation head-on in a [Feb. 22 Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DGZDXqOPY20/) video post.

 [![Image 5: Coachella, California October 12, 2024-Presidential candidate Donald Trump is introduced during a rally at Calhoun Ranch in Coachella Saturday.(Wally Skalij/Los Angeles Times)](https://ca-times.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c7792c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4434x2956+114+0/resize/840x560!/quality/75/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcalifornia-times-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2F78%2Fc6%2F9eac7d1d4310863cf2da86305ef8%2F1478516-pol-1012-trump-coachella-wjs0024.jpg)](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-10-16/trump-cognitive-ability-rally-music)

### [Column: I’m also sick of discussing Trump’s madness. But we have to](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-10-16/trump-cognitive-ability-rally-music)

Trump’s recent comments and his decision to just listen to music at a rally provided the starkest picture yet of his waning mental acuity.

Oct. 16, 2024

“We are migrants, our parents are migrants. And we want to tell you directly that we don’t support any political party that is against migrants,” Peña Jr. began the video. “With that said, there have been many things said about us that are not true.”

The band’s bajo quinto player Alberto Acosta then addressed the “false news” that had been circulated online about the “un x100to” artists. “We are doing this \[video\] because people are putting us against our raza,” Acosta said.

Advertisement

“For example the ‘Y.M.C.A’ dance, we had a routine before shows during our last tour where we’d dance a huapango or another song,” band accordionist Juan Javier Cantú said. “We’ve danced to that song since primary school and it had nothing to do with any political party at that point.”

Lead singer Adelaido “Payo” Solís proceeded to talk about a [TikTok video](https://www.tiktok.com/@sarahjasmine__/video/7465216725319945502) showing his grandmother dancing to “Y.M.C.A.” in apparent support for Trump. (Trump was not mentioned by name at any point in the video.)

### [Regional Mexican acts contributed millions of dollars at L.A.’s venues post-pandemic](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2024-09-19/grupo-firme-los-bukis-sofi-stadium-crypto-arena-fuerza-regida)

Grupo Firme’s seven record-breaking L.A. concerts in 2021 highlight Southern California’s influential place in the globally ascending música Mexicana genre.

Sept. 19, 2024

“I want to tell you all that the only opinions that count from Grupo Frontera are those that come from the group itself,” Solís said. “Any person that’s not one of the six members of Grupo Frontera can’t have an opinion on our behalf, nor speak for us, nor express our emotions.”

Peña Jr. slammed home the group’s intents with his closing statements.

“We are migrants. We’re for migrants. We always have been,” he concluded. “You guys know what we’ve done and have supported our raza in the U.S. and Mexico and wherever we are. That’s what this group represents, not what’s been said about us.”

The Times has reached out to Grupo Frontera’s representatives for comment.

HARLINGEN, Texas ([ValleyCentral](https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fvalleycentral.com%2F&data=05%7C02%7CMMorales%40kveo.com%7C8d809e3ac8a7437643d408dd4887cc41%7C9e5488e2e83844f6886cc7608242767e%7C0%7C0%7C638746470288064886%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=eTElGxsFhlFpXrpUNDFl%2FTehEdu8J%2F67%2BYKMAlJsSq8%3D&reserved=0)) — The popular Norteño group, Grupo Frontera, has responded to allegations of their affiliations endorsing President Donald Trump.

For weeks on social media, especially TikTok, videos have been circulating accusing Grupo Frontera of supporting Trump.

Many fans were outraged by the allegations and have even set up a [petition on change.org](https://nam11.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.change.org%2Fp%2Fremove-grupo-frontera-from-sue%25C3%25B1os-lineup&data=05%7C02%7CMMorales%40kveo.com%7C8d809e3ac8a7437643d408dd4887cc41%7C9e5488e2e83844f6886cc7608242767e%7C0%7C0%7C638746470288078751%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=7RojU3WFhDkh8Hmc41w9gVqNrtdH2XoBi1r2C%2Bm9YQw%3D&reserved=0) to remove the group from the Sueño Music Festival in Chicago.

The petition states, “Grupo Frontera has been caught and found out to be Trump Supporters. This does not sit well with Latinos who may or may not be fans of the group but will not support Racism.”

The statement also added, “We Latinos stand united in boycotting Grupo Frontera and if they are not removed from the line-up, we will go as far as Boycotting Sueños Music Festival as well.”

On Friday evening, Grupo Frontera broke their silence by posting on social media a statement clearing up the allegations.

“_Queremos aclarar que en Grupo Frontera NO tenemos afiliación con ningún partido político que este en contra de los inmigrantes y la comunidad latina_,” the statement reads.

The quote is translated to “We want to clarify that Grupo Frontera does NOT affiliate with any political party that is against the immigrant or Latin community.”

In the statement, they added that just like many of their fans, their families and members have fought for a better future and will forever be on the side of their people, defending their roots and values.

“_Es importante que sepan que las opiniones de familiares y amigos no representan a Grupo Frontera._” The group said. “_Nosotros somos inmigrantes somos de la frontera, y Grupo Frontera siempre sera de su gente y para su gente_.”

Their quote translates to, ” It is important for you all to know that the opinions of our families and friends do not represent Grupo Frontera. We are immigrants, we are from the border and Grupo Frontera will always be of its people and for its people.”

The members have shared this statement on their Instagram stories.

From canceled visas to protests nationwide, Ivan Cornejo, Chiquis and others are using their influence to resist strict immigration policies and stand up against ICE.

6/18/2025

The L.A. raids coupled by the Trump administration’s immigration policies have sent shockwaves through the Latin music world and beyond, bringing cultural and political tensions to the forefront.

Over the weekend, more than five million people took to the streets across the U.S. as part of the massive “No Kings” rallies. The demonstrations come amidst abrupt visa issues [disrupting major touring schedules](https://www.billboard.com/pro/regional-mexican-music-visa-issues-trump-administration/) for Mexican stars like Julión Álvarez and Grupo Firme, and Donald Trump’s deployment of 2,000 [California National Guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N5P_XzIGZ4k) troops to quell protests. The stakes have never been higher.

Latin artists — many of whom are immigrants or come from immigrant families — are using their platforms to speak out against these injustices and stand in solidarity with affected communities.

In the face of increased ICE raids, revoked visas, and inflammatory rhetoric, stars like [Ivan Cornejo](https://www.billboard.com/artist/ivan-cornejo/), [Fuerza Regida](https://www.billboard.com/artist/fuerza-regida/), [Chiquis](https://www.billboard.com/artist/chiquis-rivera/) and more are delivering hope and empowerment. “The people being attacked today are not ‘illegal aliens’, they are human beings with RIGHTS,” wrote [Becky G](https://www.billboard.com/artist/becky-g/) on Instagram. “We must understand that an attack on them is an attack on OUR DEMOCRACY and an attack on what this country was made to stand for.”

“It no longer feels like the country of hope they told us so much about,” added [DannyLux](https://www.billboard.com/artist/dannylux/).

Their activism doesn’t stop at words. Many have donated to community organizations and shared resources, such as Cornejo and Cuco with [CHIRLA.org](https://www.chirla.org/) (Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights); and [Peso Pluma](https://www.billboard.com/artist/peso-pluma/) and his manager George Prajin’s labels Double P Records and Prajin Parlay, who shared links to immigrant rights organizations: [ilrc.org](https://www.ilrc.org/red-cards-tarjetas-rojas?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=1569317919&gbraid=0AAAAADouz7_vSA_L0YGkXZoieccaBanZ0&gclid=CjwKCAjw9anCBhAWEiwAqBJ-cxgHoXNgpp9UX-jFnkvmZxnwh-pSzqWjh13My6dQPD24p4i9yZyCvhoC5P8QAvD_BwE) (Immigrant Legal Recourse Center), [Nilc.org](https://www.nilc.org/) (National Immigration Law Center), [UnitedWeDream.org](https://unitedwedream.org/) and more.

“The peaceful and non violent fight for justice, dignity, and humanity for our immigrant community is one we are proud to be part of,” the two aforementioned labels [wrote](https://www.instagram.com/stories/doubleprecords/3652975608230982165/?igsh=MThlN2JvaWNxZWtpNA%3D%3D).

Underground punk scenes like L.A.’s DIY Hardcore movement have even raised $10K for the city’s undocumented families affected by ICE. “We’re in crisis mode,” Victor Campos, the Director of Mosh for Youth, [told](https://lataco.com/hardcore-scene-fundraise-against-ice) _[L.A. Taco](https://lataco.com/hardcore-scene-fundraise-against-ice)._ “Immigrants build our communities, and they thrive with immigrants. If we look at who’s being taken by the raids, it’s hard-working Latinos. They’re going to Home Depots, to swap meets, to places of business, and taking our people away. Families are left broken and shattered by these raids, so it’s our responsibility as individuals with platforms to do something about it.”

The growing wave of Latin artists using their platforms to push back against Trump’s immigration policies also includes [Maná](https://www.billboard.com/artist/mana/), [Don Omar](https://www.billboard.com/artist/don-omar/), [Pepe Aguilar](https://www.billboard.com/artist/pepe-aguilar/). Check out how they’re speaking out with messages of resilience to inspire action. (In alphabetical order.)

*   Ángela Aguilar
    --------------
    
    ![Image 1: Feature, Women in Music, Ángela Aguilar](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/feature-angela-aguilar-billboard-2025-bb5-pooneh-ghana-3-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Pooneh Ghana
    
    Ángela Aguilar has been speaking out about the migration crisis, saying she feels she has “a responsibility,” as she shared with _Billboard_ in a [video posted](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/angela-aguilar-producing-album-immigration-crisis-1235993718/) on June 10. At the Billboard Women in Music 2024 event, the 21-year-old singer was honored with the Breakthrough Award and gave a heartfelt speech about immigrant rights.
    
    “It’s very taboo to talk about things like that in awards and just anywhere,” [she said](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/angela-aguilar-breakthrough-award-billboard-women-in-music-1235934965/). “And people tell you not to do it but again, I have a responsibility as a Mexican American to speak about injustices that are going on because it directly affects my people, people that go to my concerts and consume my music. There’s nothing worse than to not have a voice and to have people speak for you.”
    
*   Bad Bunny
    ---------
    
    ![Image 2: Bad Bunny performs onstage at the 2025 iHeartRadio Music Awards at Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, California on March 17, 2025. Broadcasted live on FOX. (Photo by Kevin Winter/Getty Images for iHeartRadio)](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/bad-bunny-iheartradio-music-awards-2025-billboard-02-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Winter/Getty Images
    
    Bad Bunny has voiced his frustration with the Trump administration’s latest actions in Puerto Rico. In a video he shared on his [Instagram Story](https://www.instagram.com/stories/badbunnypr/?hl=en) on Tuesday (June 17), the [Puerto Rican artist condemned](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/bad-bunny-video-slams-ice-immigration-raids-puerto-rico-1236001925/) what he claimed was ICE raid in his homeland of Puerto Rico. “Those motherf–kers are in these cars, RAV4’s. They came here… sons of b–ches, instead of letting the people alone and working,” he said in his clip while in the Avenida Pontezuela in Carolina, Puerto Rico.
    
*   Becky G
    -------
    
    ![Image 3: Becky G](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Becky-G-coachella-2025-billboard-a-8-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for Coachella
    
    For Becky G, activism is personal. As the proud granddaughter of immigrants, the singer took to Instagram to share an emotionally charged post emphasizing the humanity of immigrant communities and the importance of treating them with dignity and respect. “The people being attacked today are not ‘illegal aliens’, they are human beings with RIGHTS,” she wrote on Instagram. “We must understand that an attack on them is an attack on OUR DEMOCRACY and an attack on what this country was made to stand for.”
    
    She continued, “We want safety and protection for our immigrant community — in a country where the right to protest, peacefully, has consistently changed the course of history. Our hearts are broken but our spirit & will to fight back is not!” The Inglewood native also revealed she has been “donating, speaking with organizers, and gathering reliable, immediate resources and information” with those affected by ICE raids and protests.
    
*   Chiquis
    -------
    
    ![Image 4: Chiquis](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Chiquis-billboard-wim-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: John Parra/Telemundo via Getty Images
    
    Chiquis Rivera has voiced her solidarity with immigrants in the U.S., offering words of caution and support. In an interview shared on the program _Sale el Sol_ from Imagen Televisión on Tuesday (June 10), the singer warned, “There is going to be ICE everywhere. So if you don’t have papers, I suggest you stay home.”
    
    She continued, “Do your best not to go out for the next 30 days if you don’t have to…think about what might happen tomorrow.”
    
*   Cuco
    ----
    
    ![Image 5: Cuco](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Cuco-cr-Carlos-Jaramillo-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Carlos Jaramillo
    
    Cuco has also utilized his [Instagram Story](https://www.instagram.com/stories/cucopuffs/) to share a variety of videos in support of immigrants and condemning ICE, including a bold “F–K ICE” statement. Following his outspoken criticism, the artist shared the some outright racist messages and supporting ones he received in response. He also provided a range of resources to support affected communities, including [merch sales](https://www.instagram.com/p/DLA0sQDvHhH/) with 100% of profits going to Chirla.org.
    
    In addition, the Hawthorn, California artist shared videos highlighting instances of ICE arresting U.S. citizens of Latin origin; and promoted Caló News, a [platform that tracks ICE sightings](https://www.calonews.com/featured-topics/immigration/how-to-track-ice/article_d9e1039d-c00f-4e42-840e-3eb9e51974f1.html). This resource allows families, allies, and immigrants to access maps and gather updates on ICE activity in their area.
    
    He spotlighted a hotline created by USC law students (888-462-5211) to assist individuals with immigrant-related court hearings. This hotline helps people who fear arrest or detention outside courthouses to complete and submit a “Motion to Change Hearing Format,” enabling them to attend court remotely or online instead of in person.
    
*   DannyLux
    --------
    
    ![Image 6: DannyLux](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/DannyLux-cr-Sean-Behr-press-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Sean Behr
    
    “My dad came to this country illegally at 17 years old with the dream that his children would have a better future… like many of our parents,” wrote DannyLux on an Instagram post. He lamented the harassment of Latin communities, especially in L.A., while reflecting on the struggles of immigrant families.
    
    “It hurts me so much to see everything that’s happening in Los Angeles and throughout the Nation. It no longer feels like the country of hope they told us so much about,” the Mexican-American artist continued, highlighting the disconnect between the idealized image of the U.S. and the harsh realities immigrant communities are currently facing. The artist recognized the protests as “a cry from a community tired of being ignored and criminalized just for seeking that dignified life!”
    
*   Devendra Banhanrt
    -----------------
    
    ![Image 7: Devendra Banhart performs at The Fillmore on Jan. 26, 2017 in San Francisco.](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/media/Devendra-Banhart-2016-performance-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Tim Mosenfelder/Getty Images
    
    Devendra Banhart, freak-folk artist, has also added his voice to the discourse surrounding immigration policies and their real-life impact under the Trump’s administration. “The surreal and horrifying shock of what’s happening in this community is heartbreaking… the outrage and strength of everyone’s resistance is so powerful,” he wrote on Instagram, while posting a flyer of Defend Immigrants’ California Rapid Response Networks to provide resources and emergency assistance during ICE raids.
    
    As someone born in the U.S. but raised in Venezuela, he highlighted “I’ve seen firsthand what corruption and cruelty does when gone unchecked … _sigan luchando hermanas y hermanos_ (keep fighting brothers and sisters).”
    
*   Don Omar
    --------
    
    ![Image 8: Don Omar](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Don-Omar-Performs-At-Coca-Cola-Coliseum-march-2024-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Jeremychanphotography/Getty Images
    
    Don Omar shared a heartfelt message on an Instagram video, celebrating the resilience and hope that define the immigrant experience in the U.S. “There is something very beautiful about being an immigrant, and that very beautiful thing about being an immigrant is the desire to improve oneself,” the reggaetón icon said.
    
    “It is time for all of us migrants and immigrants to come together, we must see ourselves as one people,” said the Puerto Rican artist, urging them to view themselves as one unified pueblo. See the clip below.
    
*   Eslabon Armado
    --------------
    
    ![Image 9: Eslabon Armado](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Eslabon-Armado-cr-Armado-Publishing-LLC-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Armado Publishing LLC
    
    Mexican-American band Eslabón Armado has demonstrated its solidarity with families and the Hispanic community of Los Angeles during turbulent times marked by anti-Latino rhetoric from the presidency. In a [live stream video](https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/d5z4yrd9sykiijpiz8egu/Eslabon-Armado-LA-Events-Video-2025-06-13.mp4?rlkey=8yyt1j6kxal6kyhd3y9p5easn&e=1&st=7j1yf6y7&dl=0) shared with _Billboard Español_, frontman Pedro Tovar expressed his sadness and frustration over the events affecting families and the immigrant community of Southern California.
    
    “It’s sad seeing all of our people being treated like s–t, and for that reason, we’re going to do a special show in L.A. with three other artists that you guys know and love,” he said, announcing that Eslabón Armado will participate in a charity event, with donations going directly to families impacted by recent events.
    
*   Fuerza Regida
    -------------
    
    ![Image 10: Fuerza Regida](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Fuerza-Regida-cr-Courtesy-of-Street-Mob-Records-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Courtesy of Street Mob Records
    
    Fuerza Regida, alongside their label Street Mob Records, sent a message of solidarity via social media to their fanbase amid the current immigration crackdown. “We’re sending love and strength to our Latino communities during this difficult time,” they wrote. “These are our people, our fans, the very communities that inspire our music. We see your strength and resilience.”
    
    The band further expressed their commitment to action, revealing plans to support those directly impacted by these events. “Stay safe, stay strong, and remember, _juntos podemos lograr todo_,” they added.
    
    And [as JOP says](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DK3a1gixA3p/?igsh=YTIzNGV6YTd1b2di): “And remember my people that ICE always melts!”
    
*   Grupo Frontera
    --------------
    
    ![Image 11: Grupo Frontera photographed December 20, 2024 in McAllen, Texas.](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/cover-groupo-frontera-billboard-espanol-2025-bb4-jasmine-archie-1-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Jasmine Archie
    
    Known for their cross-border appeal and cultural pride, Grupo Frontera is clear in their resolve: they will not stop fighting for their people. In an Instagram story, the border band showed their solidarity for immigrant communities facing hardship and discrimination across the U.S.
    
    “We’re watching everything that’s happening in Los Angeles, Texas, and across the country, and we want you to know that you’re not alone,” [they wrote](https://www.instagram.com/stories/grupofrontera/3652784345953228896/?hl=en). “As immigrants, we understand the pain, uncertainty, and fear that many are experiencing. It hurts to see our people go through this, and that’s why we want to speak out.”
    
    “Now more than ever, it’s time to come together, to look out for one another, and to keep moving towards dignity and hope. We continue to show our solidarity with our community, because your well-being is what matters most to us,” they added.
    
    Grupo Frontera is also donating a portion of all proceeds from their surprise EP _Y Lo Que Viene_, released Friday (June 13) to frontline organizations supporting the community.
    
*   Ivan Cornejo
    ------------
    
    ![Image 12: Ivan Cornejo](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/ivan-cornejo-press-credit-Le3ay-Studio-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Le3ay Studio
    
    Ivan Cornejo shared a message reflecting his personal connection to the struggles faced by immigrants today. “America was built on the backs of immigrants like my father, and now we’re being targeted, undermining America’s core values,” the Mexican-American artist wrote in a statement.
    
    The singer, whose father was granted amnesty in 1986 under then-President Ronald Reagan, spoke of the cultural and economic contributions immigrants have always made to the country, while expressing sorrow over the current political climate. He emphasized his commitment to using his art as a form of solidarity and launched efforts to raise funds for immigrant advocacy organizations such as CHIRLA.
    
*   Jimmy Humilde
    -------------
    
    ![Image 13: Jimmy Humilde at Featured Session "The Rise of Rancho Humilde with Jimmy Humilde" during SXSW Conference & Festivals at Austin Convention Center on March 12, 2025 in Austin, Texas.](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/sxsw-jimmy-humilde-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Amanda Stronza
    
    Jimmy Humilde, the founder of Rancho Humilde, shared a poetic message that celebrates unity and resilience within the Mexican-American community. “United we rise. Together we stand, hand in hand, Mexican and American, united we band,” the poem begins.
    
    His message reminds us that, even in times of political and social pressure, the strength of community and shared heritage can inspire hope and collective action. Read his full message below.
    
*   Junior H
    --------
    
    ![Image 14: Junior H](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/Junior-H-2024-Arre-Festival-in-Mexico-City-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Ocesa/Liliana Estrada
    
    Junior H is leveraging his influence beyond music to advocate for justice. “We’re living through tough times. We can’t stay silent while our communities are being attacked. This is my way of giving back and standing with the people who’ve always stood by me,” he shared about his latest merch drop.
    
    The música mexicana star announced that 100 percent of profits from the collection will benefit chirla.org, a nonprofit dedicated to providing legal support to immigrants facing ICE detention and deportation.
    
*   Maná
    ----
    
    ![Image 15: Fher Olvera and Sergio Vallín of Maná perform onstage during 2024 BottleRock Napa Valley at Napa Valley Expo on May 25, 2024 in Napa, California.](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/mana-bottlerock-napa-2024-21-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Mazur/WireImage
    
    “People like you, the only thing you have done is to work and work, and make this country great,” Fher Olvera, frontman of the legendary Mexican rock band Maná, hold his immigrant following in an Instagram video, acknowledging the countless contributions of Latinos to the U.S. “Don’t give these foos any excuses to take advantage of you or call you criminals and thugs. Protest peacefully so you don’t give these guys any reason to blame you. \[…\] That’s how you’ll win.”
    
    The Guadalajara singer-songwriter urged his audience to reject violence and protest peacefully, particularly those facing hardships in L.A.
    
    Olvera, alongside Maná, have long been defenders of immigrants in the United States, often fostering solidarity during performances and beyond.
    
*   Nezza
    -----
    
    ![Image 16: Nezza](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/nezza-may-12-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Vivien Killilea/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures
    
    Nezza, a Colombian-Dominican Latin pop singer raised in California’s Bay Area, was invited to sing the U.S. national anthem at a recent Dodgers vs. Giants game at Dodger Stadium in L.A. However, instead of performing it in English as reportedly instructed, the singer delivered a Spanish-language version of the anthem, dedicating it “_para mi gente_ \[for my people\],” she shared on Sunday (June 15).
    
    The clip shows footage of Nezza [on the baseball field singing](https://www.tiktok.com/@hernandezla/video/7516005711562935598) “The Star-Spangled Banner” in Spanish, “El Pendón Estrellado.” “I didn’t think I would be met with any sort of ‘no,’ especially because we’re in L.A., and with everything happening … I just could not believe when she walked in and told me ‘no.’ I just felt like I needed to do it,” Nezza said in a video.
    
*   Pepe Aguilar
    ------------
    
    ![Image 17: Pepe Aguilar](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/pepe-aguilar-press-credit-Constanza-Martinez-2024-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Constanza Martinez
    
    The iconic Mexican artist shared his perspective on the realities facing immigrant communities during these challenging times, emphasizing unity and dignity as tools for overcoming adversity.
    
    “One has to keep going and keep working, doing one’s best to keep doing things with the utmost dignity and pride,” he expressed in a heartfelt video. Pepe Aguilar underscored the importance of remaining united, as he believes collective strength can help “reverse any situation.”
    
    In line with his values, Aguilar offered a sneak peek at an unreleased song that captures the perspective of the immigrant experience. “\[It is\] a peaceful resistance with art, with memory, with culture, with tradition,” he said. “It has to do with traditions, with Mexico, not forgetting where we come from and who we are.”
    
*   Peso Pluma
    ----------
    
    ![Image 18: Peso Pluma](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/peso-pluma-2025-suenos-festival-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Courtesy of Sueños/@diegoguillen
    
    Peso Pluma is taking action to support immigrant communities during a time of distress and fear. He shared a statement from Double P Records and Prajin Parlay on [his Instagram story](https://www.instagram.com/stories/pesopluma/), providing information from organizations that help immigrants navigate these times of uncertainty (see links in the introduction).
    
    “We are deeply heartbroken over what is happening in Los Angeles and all across the country. This country was built by our ancestors, hard working immigrants who came to this country to build a better life for us,” says the statement. “As children of immigrants and immigrants ourselves, we know this struggle personally. We know the strength it takes to build a life, to sacrifice everything for a better future, and to keep moving forward even when the odds are stacked against you.”
    
*   Shakira
    -------
    
    ![Image 19: Shakira](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/shakira-grammys-rc-2025-billboard-3-espanol-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Gilbert Flores
    
    Shakira [opened up](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/shakira-immigrant-us-trump-policies-live-in-constant-fear-1235999720/) about her experiences as an immigrant living in the U.S. amid President Donald Trump’s immigration policies. In an [interview](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn056ky4d00o) with the BBC, Colombian-born superstar reflected on the challenges and fear faced by immigrant communities today, describing moving to Miami at age 19 to pursue a music career.
    
    “It means living in constant fear,” Shakira told the BBC when asked what it’s like to be an immigrant in the U.S. today. “And it’s painful to see.” As a longtime advocate for social justice, she has voiced concerns about the intensified ICE raids and deportations under Trump’s administration. “Now, more than ever, we have to remain united,” she said, adding, “Now, more than ever, we have to raise our voices and make it very clear that a country can change its immigration policies, but the treatment of all people must always be humane.”
    
*   Snow Tha Product
    ----------------
    
    ![Image 20: Snow Tha Product](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/snow-tha-product-press-credit-Ulises-Ceron-2024-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Ulises Ceron
    
    Snow Tha Product, the unapologetic rapper and vocal advocate for immigrant rights, weighed in on the political climate surrounding immigration policies and protest movements. Offering a sharp critique of the government’s tactics, she urged, “We need to be smart right now. They want us to act up so they can shut everything down. This man wants to shut everything down, that’s his goal. His goal is to end up dictating without looking like that was his plan from the beginning.”
    
    “All these little knuckleheads out here, they’re going to start vandalizing, tagging s–t, doing stupid s–t, and it’s going to f–k up the movement,” she stated bluntly. Her message is clear: the fight for justice demands strategy and discipline to ensure that resistance remains powerful and effective.
    
*   Los Tigres del Norte
    --------------------
    
    ![Image 21: Los Tigres del Norte](https://www.billboard.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Los-Tigres-del-Norte-cr-Fonovisa-2025-billboard-1548.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Fonovisa Records
    
    The legendary norteño figures have long used their songs to champion social justice and give voice to immigrant communities in the United States. Known for classics like “De Paisano a Paisano” and “Somos Más Americanos,” the band’s music often highlights the struggles and resilience of those seeking a better life across borders.
    
    Reflecting on their mission, lead vocalist Jorge Hernández [recently told](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/los-tigres-del-norte-doesnt-fear-retaliation-donald-trump-retaliation-1235898927/) _Billboard Español_, “I think it comes at a time when we were already seeing what was coming.” Staying true to their roots, Los Tigres have continuously advocated for immigrants. “We did what we had to do as human beings and as citizens of this country and as citizens of our Mexican Republic,” Hernández added. “We will continue to move forward fighting for those people who have no voice.”
    
    Their advocacy was recently recognized when Los Tigres del Norte were honored by the Monterey County Board of Supervisors, receiving Lifetime Recognition for their decades of work on behalf of immigrants. At a ceremony in Salinas, the band was awarded the key to the County of Monterey, as well as a resolution declaring June 10 as “Los Tigres del Norte Day” in Monterey County.

![Image 1: Grupo Frontera](https://s.yimg.com/ny/api/res/1.2/xHdt.bfqYuluUtfGjZoinQ--/YXBwaWQ9aGlnaGxhbmRlcjt3PTcwNTtoPTg4MTtjZj13ZWJw/https://media.zenfs.com/en/la_times_de_los_699/7c645292db0a66176ba244814ef4e4d7)

(Elana Marie / De Los; photo by Elina Adut / The Exclusive Agency)

Grupo Frontera gets that people want to ask them about the U.S.-Mexico border: look at their name and look at the current [political climate](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2025-03-05/trumps-address-to-congress-revived-false-or-misleading-claims-on-immigration). They mostly just don't want to talk about that.

But behind the line of questioning have been the [rumors](https://www.tiktok.com/@alexgootz/video/7465856247015755013) [swirling](https://www.tiktok.com/@aldoandheather/video/7465286279681428782) [online](https://www.tiktok.com/@alondracosilionn/video/7468870894442532102) that the Grupo Frontera members and those related to its members voted for and supported President Trump in the 2024 presidential election. The speculation has forced the "Tulum" performers to deny any affiliations with any political parties several times over.

So ahead of the Norteño band's upcoming gig at SXSW on March 14, here's a refresher of turbulent 2025 online discourse the Texas artists have found themselves at the center of.

In an interview with [Billboard](https://www.billboard.com/music/latin/grupo-frontera-sxsw-billboard-cover-1235914782/) published Tuesday, the group was asked whether or not its felt the effects of the political moment.

“I mean, our group name, Grupo Frontera, I think it feels natural for people to be like, ‘You’re from the border,’ stuff like that,” drummer Carlos Guerrero said in section of the interview that was notably conducted in December. “We always try to keep that private.” Percussionist Julian Peña Jr. added the group aims to "talk about music, that’s it."

But this was far from the first time the "No Se Va" singers have been asked about or been placed in a situation where they've been forced to talk about the U.S. political situation. It does, however, follow a pattern of nondescript answers that the group's members have previously been provided.

**Read more:** [The Música Mexicana revolution shaping Southern California](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2024-09-19/the-musica-mexicana-revolution-shaping-socal?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)

In a now-deleted TikTok video that circulated earlier this year, Grupo Frontera was shown dancing to the Village People's mega hit "Y.M.C.A." This concerned fans of the band online because of the song's heavy association with [Donald Trump rallies](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-10-16/trump-cognitive-ability-rally-music), which the politician has used at his events since [at least 2020](https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/tv/story/2020-10-19/trump-dancing-rally-seinfeld-julia-louis-dreyfus).

Around the time that the "Y.M.C.A." video circulated, Grupo Frontera was announced as the headliners at the Sueños music festival in Chicago. Soon after the announcement, a [Change.org petition](https://www.change.org/p/remove-grupo-frontera-from-sue%C3%B1os-lineup) was started that called for the band to be removed from the festival lineup and has collected over 10,400 signatures.

The Chicago man who started the online campaign said he paid over $800 and wanted a refund due to what he believed was the band's shift in ideology, according to the [Chicago-Sun Times](https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/suenos-music-festival-chicago/2025/02/11/grupo-frontera-trump-suenos-petition-festival-chicago-ymca). The man admitted that the video of the group dancing to "Y.M.C.A" did not mention Trump or express any overt political views, but he noted that the timing of the post felt significant to him.

**Read more:** [Even 'Seinfeld' cast thinks Trump's awkward dance moves are worse than Elaine's](https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/tv/story/2020-10-19/trump-dancing-rally-seinfeld-julia-louis-dreyfus?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)

Following the circulation of the video, the group's social media posts became filled with comments such as: "You guys should start singing in English," "In Mexico we don't forgive," and "Let's stop supporting a group that is anti-Mexican."

The hitmakers seemingly responded to the online backlash they were receiving in a social media post.

“We want to clarify that Grupo Frontera has NO affiliation not alliance with any political party that’s against immigrants and the Latino community,” the group wrote in a Feb. 7 Instagram story. “Like many of you, our families and \[group\] members have fought and struggled for a better future, and we will always take our people’s side, defending our roots and values.”

The band continued, “It’s important you know that the opinions of our friends and family don’t represent Grupo Frontera. We are immigrants, we are from the border, and Grupo Frontera will always be by and for the people."

(Trump was not mentioned in the band's statement.)

![Image 2: Grupo Frontera during a press conference at the Microsoft Theater in Los Angeles on February 16, 2023. Photo by James Carbone](https://s.yimg.com/ny/api/res/1.2/Ewt3J9MKn5ojLRd8HAT2pA--/YXBwaWQ9aGlnaGxhbmRlcjt3PTk2MDtoPTY1MjtjZj13ZWJw/https://media.zenfs.com/en/la_times_de_los_699/a563171334d89c040caabf65171ded1a)

(James Carbone)

A few weeks later while on the red carpet at the Premios Lo Nuestro on Feb. 20, TV presenter [Raul De Molina](https://www.latimes.com/espanol/entretenimiento/articulo/2025-02-27/el-gordo-y-la-flaca-develan-sus-estrellas-en-compania-de-los-estefan-y-thalia) asked Grupo Frontera, "You guys are named 'border,' what do you think about the what is happening at the border between the U.S. and Mexico?"

**Read more:** [How a carne asada changed the lives of Grupo Frontera](https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/newsletter/2023-05-04/latinx-files-grupo-frontera-bad-bunny-un-x100to-coachella-puro-956-cuh-latinx-files?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)

"We dedicate ourselves to music. We love everyone and want peace and love. Take care of yourselves," Peña Jr. responded.

Social media personality and immigrant rights activist [Carlos Eduardo Espina](https://www.tiktok.com/@carlos_eduardo_espina), who touts 12.3 million TikTok followers, was among the [many](https://www.tiktok.com/@antonioamex1/video/7465406578057940255) [people](https://www.tiktok.com/@therealkatherine/video/7465576786303208747) [upset](https://x.com/suaonthemoon/status/1884661389781786645) online and responded to the clip of the red carpet moment with a loud condemnation of Peña Jr.'s comments.

"For me, this was one of the worst responses that I have ever seen to a question in my whole life," Espina said in a [Feb. 21 TikTok video](https://www.tiktok.com/@carlos_eduardo_espina/video/7473892359663652126). "Just like the saying goes, there are times when not saying anything says a lot. ... what an embarrassment."

Following that round of online criticism Grupo Frontera decided to address the situation head-on in a [Feb. 22 Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DGZDXqOPY20/) video post.

**Read more:** [Column: I'm also sick of discussing Trump's madness. But we have to](https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-10-16/trump-cognitive-ability-rally-music?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)

"We are migrants, our parents are migrants. And we want to tell you directly that we don't support any political party that is against migrants," Peña Jr. began the video. "With that said, there have been many things said about us that are not true."

The band's bajo quinto player Alberto Acosta then addressed the "false news" that had been circulated online about the "un x100to" artists. "We are doing this \[video\] because people are putting us against our raza,” Acosta said.

"For example the 'Y.M.C.A' dance, we had a routine before shows during our last tour where we'd dance a huapango or another song," band accordionist Juan Javier Cantú said. "We've danced to that song since primary school and it had nothing to do with any political party at that point."

Lead singer Adelaido "Payo" Solís proceeded to talk about a [TikTok video](https://www.tiktok.com/@sarahjasmine__/video/7465216725319945502) showing his grandmother dancing to "Y.M.C.A." in apparent support for Trump. (Trump was not mentioned by name at any point in the video.)

**Read more:** [Regional Mexican acts contributed millions of dollars at L.A.’s venues post-pandemic](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2024-09-19/grupo-firme-los-bukis-sofi-stadium-crypto-arena-fuerza-regida?utm_source=yahoo&utm_medium=promo_module&utm_campaign=rss_feed)

"I want to tell you all that the only opinions that count from Grupo Frontera are those that come from the group itself," Solís said. "Any person that's not one of the six members of Grupo Frontera can't have an opinion on our behalf, nor speak for us, nor express our emotions."

Peña Jr. slammed home the group's intents with his closing statements.

“We are migrants. We’re for migrants. We always have been,” he concluded. “You guys know what we’ve done and have supported our raza in the U.S. and Mexico and wherever we are. That’s what this group represents, not what’s been said about us.”

The Times has reached out to Grupo Frontera's representatives for comment.
